title: The Language of Belonging
author: David Didau
summary: Belonging is linguistic, not pastoral. The mainstream literature treats belonging as an emotional microclimate that warm adults create for children to bask in or shiver at the margins of. Didau argues instead that school runs through talk at every level (lessons, corridors, feedback) carrying specific grammar, cadence, and academic assumptions. Children who can enter that discourse feel like insiders; children who cannot stay on the fringes no matter how warm the adults. Standard instruments miss this because they measure perceptions of care without examining the medium through which those perceptions form. The move is to stop treating belonging as separate from academic work, and start treating explicit teaching of academic language as a belonging intervention. Children need fluency in specialized school language, yes, but they also need to recognize themselves as members of the communities that use it. The teaching has to be explicit and the membership has to be named.
points: Belonging is linguistic, not emotional: children feel like insiders or outsiders based on whether they can fluently enter the academic discourse that runs through every lesson and interaction.
Warm adult relationships matter, but they cannot overcome the effect of academic language that children cannot understand; the medium through which perceptions of care are formed is discourse itself.
Explicit teaching of academic language is a belonging intervention, not merely an achievement strategy.
Children need to recognize themselves as members of the communities that use academic language; belonging requires that membership be named, not just assumed.
quotes: If you were not worried about belonging before the new Ofsted framework, you are now. The new inspection toolkit defines belong as one of three core lenses through which inspectors will evaluate a school.

Under the 2025 framework, inclusion, with belonging folded into it, becomes a discrete area of evaluation. Inspectors expect schools to show how they notice and respond to those who meet resistance in the system.

Most writing about belonging treats it as a kind of emotional weather system that drifts over children and shapes their commitment to school. As long we focus, so the logic goes, on warm relationships, smiles in corridors and signals of care all will be well.
This absence is odd because the lived experience of school, and every other aspect of life, is linguistic from start to finish. To belong is to feel able to take part in its conversations.
The corridors are thick with talk, and much of that talk is academic in character. It has a grammar, a cadence and a set of tacit assumptions. You either understand or you do not.

Yet for all its impressive scope, the study also exposes the blind spot that runs through almost the entire field. It tracks social bonds, perceptions of care and the sense that adults in school notice what children do.

Now, I would go further: To be academically successful, children need not just to be fluent in the language of academic success, but to recognize themselves as belonging within the communities that use it.” Archived from David Didau on April 20, 2026 by Tim.
